edits.walkthrough_append: **EXAM TRAP:** A licence is PERMISSION over an automatic COPYRIGHT — owning a copy is not owning the code — and licence TYPES answer different questions: GPL (copyleft, derivatives stay free), MIT/BSD (permissive, near-free), proprietary (use under restrictions); confusing "free for cost" with "free to modify" — freeware versus free software — is the standard licensing slip.

**EXAM TRAP:** OOAD analysis marks NOUNS as candidate CLASSES and VERBS as candidate METHODS — then filters out nouns that are mere attributes (colour is a field, not a class); keeping every noun as a class over-structures the design, and skipping the filtering step is exactly the modelling error the marking scheme checks.

**EXAM TRAP:** A variable is NAMED, TYPED storage — the type fixes the legal values AND operations — and Java initialises fields to defaults but NOT local variables (compile error if uninitialised); declaring type-legal but logically invalid values (age = −5) is a logic error the compiler cannot catch, which is the distinction the question draws.

**EXAM TRAP:** EVERY class inherits from Object — giving toString(), equals(), hashCode() to all objects — and overriding equals() WITHOUT hashCode() breaks hash-based collections; and toString() must be OVERRIDDEN or printing shows ClassName@hashcode — calling the inherited methods "optional to exist" misreads the inheritance contract.

**EXAM TRAP:** The AI timeline anchors: 1950 Turing test, 1956 Dartmouth workshop (term coined), 1966 ELIZA, 1997 Deep Blue, 2011 Watson, 2016 AlphaGo, 2017 Transformers — and AI WINTERS followed inflated expectations (1974-80, 1987-93); dating the Dartmouth workshop to 1950 or crediting the term "AI" to Turing are the two standard chronology slips.

**EXAM TRAP:** NLP spans UNDERSTANDING (syntax, semantics, context) and GENERATION, with ambiguity as its core challenge — "bank" of a river vs bank account — resolved stepwise through tokenisation, POS tagging, parsing; and NLU (meaning) is a SUBSET of NLP (the whole pipeline); using the two terms interchangeably loses the scope mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** A chatbot must be TRAINED (on dialogue data), EVALUATED (both automated metrics and human satisfaction), and DEPLOYED with fallback-to-human paths — the training data quality caps performance (garbage in, garbage out); and rule-based chatbots match patterns without learning — calling every chatbot "AI-trained" or skipping evaluation loses the pipeline marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** A vector is an ORDERED list of numbers — position matters (runs in match 1 vs match 2 are different components) — and vector operations act ELEMENT-WISE: addition and scalar multiplication are legal, but division of vectors is not defined; treating a vector as a plain number (ignoring dimension-matching for addition) is the standard linear-algebra slip.

**EXAM TRAP:** SVD factors a matrix into U·Σ·Vᵗ — singular values in Σ are ORDERED descending, and keeping the top-k reconstructs the BEST rank-k approximation (the basis of recommender systems) — truncation LOSES information deliberately for compression/denoising; writing the factors in any order, or expecting perfect reconstruction after truncation, misses SVD's point.

**EXAM TRAP:** A dashboard UNIFIES multiple views on ONE data source so decisions come from a single cockpit — its value is cross-chart consistency, not decoration — and every chart must carry its axis, units, and time frame; mixing time frames across panels (monthly vs cumulative) creates false trends, the design flaw the dashboard question targets.

**EXAM TRAP:** Interactivity maps USER ACTIONS (hover, filter, zoom, drill-down) to DATA queries — the map must be defined before coding, and each action should REVEAL information, not just decorate; adding zoom without data refresh is cosmetic, not interactive — the action-to-data mapping is precisely what the definition asks you to show.

**EXAM TRAP:** Interactive visualisation is EXPLORATION through user-driven actions — filter, sort, zoom, drill — and its test is whether the user can answer a NEW question without the designer's help; a static chart with buttons (no data change) fails the definition, and overload with unlinked widgets fragments the exploration.

**EXAM TRAP:** Chart selection follows the QUESTION TYPE — comparison → bars, trend over time → line, part-to-whole → pie/stacked (few categories), relationship → scatter — and 3-D effects and dual axes distort perception; choosing a pie for time-series comparison, or decorating with 3-D, are the standard visualisation-choice errors.

**EXAM TRAP:** Data collection sets the CEILING — biased sampling, missing consent, or unlabelled data cannot be fixed downstream — and REPRESENTATIVENESS (the sample mirrors the population) matters more than volume; fixing a biased dataset after model training with more of the same data is exactly the garbage-in path the principle warns against.

**EXAM TRAP:** Cleaning handles MISSING values (drop, impute mean/median/mode — choice depends on missingness), DUPLICATES, OUTLIERS (investigate before deleting — they may be real), and INCONSISTENT labels; mean-imputation on skewed data drags imputed values wrong, and silent deletion of outliers can erase the signal — the choice-reasoning is what the question marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** Feature engineering CREATES informative inputs — price per square foot, age of house, distance to metro — because raw columns rarely predict directly; and EVERY feature must be computed from information available AT PREDICTION TIME — using the sale date's final price to predict that sale is leakage, the classic feature-engineering trap.

**EXAM TRAP:** Transformation makes features COMPARABLE — min-max scales to [0,1] (sensitive to outliers), z-score standardises to mean 0/SD 1 (robust for skewed data) — and SCALERS must be FITTED on training data only, then applied to test data; fitting the scaler on all data leaks test information, the standard preprocessing error.

**EXAM TRAP:** OLS minimises the SUM OF SQUARED VERTICAL errors — squared so negative and positive errors don't cancel and outliers are punished — and the line passes through (x̄, ȳ); using absolute errors (that is least-absolute-deviations), or measuring HORIZONTAL distances, answers a different regression than the one OLS defines.

**EXAM TRAP:** Evaluation quantifies ERROR (RMSE, MAE) and inspects RESIDUALS — residuals should be random with no pattern; a curved residual pattern means the model MISSES structure (try a non-linear term), and funnel-shaped residuals mean non-constant variance — a good R² with patterned residuals is still a bad model, which is exactly the trap the question sets.

**EXAM TRAP:** Residual analysis VERIFIES assumptions — residuals must be random (independence), constant-variance (homoscedasticity), and roughly normal for inference — a U-shaped residual plot signals a missing quadratic term, and systematic signs signal bias; declaring a model good from R² alone without residual inspection skips the verification step the question rewards.

**EXAM TRAP:** Privacy in a health-survey app needs INFORMED CONSENT (purpose stated), DATA MINIMISATION (collect only what's needed), anonymisation/pseudonymisation, and ACCESS CONTROL — parental consent for minors; and de-identified data can still re-identify when combined with other datasets, which is why minimisation precedes anonymisation in the design order.

**EXAM TRAP:** The three pillars are interdependent: TRANSPARENCY (how it works) enables EXPLAINABILITY (why this output) which enables ACCOUNTABILITY (who answers for it) — a black-box recommendation of fertilizer doses cannot be audited, so wrong-dose liability has no owner; treating the pillars as alternatives instead of a chain misses the trust architecture the question tests.

**EXAM TRAP:** Lab-to-farm is a STAGED pipeline — data collection, model training, field validation, deployment, monitoring — and each stage can fail differently (lab accuracy collapses on real field variability); DEPLOYMENT is not the end — monitoring for drift and farmer feedback loops back into retraining — stopping the pipeline at deployment is the incomplete-answer pattern.

**EXAM TRAP:** Self-attention lets EVERY token attend to every other token in PARALLEL (unlike sequential RNNs), with attention weights showing which words matter — enabling long-range dependencies and GPU-scale training that made LLMs possible; and Transformers still need positional ENCODINGS because attention alone is order-blind — omitting that mechanism loses the architecture's key detail.

**EXAM TRAP:** The mathematics stack maps to tasks: linear algebra (data as vectors/matrices), statistics (uncertainty), probability (prediction), calculus (learning via gradients) — and a model is only as sound as its mathematical assumptions; naming the tools without connecting each to its ML role (e.g., gradients enable training) loses the framework link the question asks for.

**EXAM TRAP:** A vector has MAGNITUDE and DIRECTION — represented by ordered components whose count is the DIMENSION — and vectors are compared by dot products (alignment) in AI similarity computations; adding vectors head-to-tail differs from adding magnitudes, and dimension mismatch makes addition illegal — the legality rules are the standard test focus.

**EXAM TRAP:** Set operations are LOGIC in data form — union (OR), intersection (AND), difference (AND NOT) — and |A∪B| = |A| + |B| − |A∩B| prevents double counting; treating overlapping sets as disjoint (skipping the intersection subtraction) is exactly the counting error the set-theory question is built to catch.

**EXAM TRAP:** Visualisation comes FIRST because it exposes OUTLIERS, distributions, and relationships before modelling — plots guide cleaning and feature choice; but a plot can MISLEAD (truncated axes, dual scales) — verifying surprises numerically before acting on a visual is the discipline the first-step rationale demands.

**EXAM TRAP:** Match the statistical graph to the data: HISTOGRAM for continuous distributions (bars TOUCH), BAR chart for categories (bars separate), BOX PLOT for median/quartiles/outliers, SCATTER for two-variable relationships; drawing a histogram with gaps (or a bar chart for ages) confuses continuous and categorical data — the pairing rule carries the mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Dimensionality reduction (PCA) compresses many correlated features into FEW uncorrelated components that retain MAXIMUM variance — it helps visualisation and fights the curse of dimensionality — but components are LINEAR COMBINATIONS, harder to interpret than original features; reading PC1 as a "real" feature, or reducing before understanding which features matter, are the standard misuse traps.

**EXAM TRAP:** Reducing dimensions to 2D/3D makes data VISUALISABLE, but the projection DISCARDS variance — close points in the plot may differ in dropped dimensions; and PCA must be FIT on scaled data (unscaled big-magnitude features dominate components); treating the 2D plot as the full truth, or skipping scaling, are the two interpretation errors the question screens.

**EXAM TRAP:** Features on different SCALES bias distance-based models (salary in rupees drowns age in years) — normalisation (min-max, bounded, outlier-sensitive) versus standardisation (z-score, robust) must be chosen per data — and the scaler fits on TRAINING data only; fitting on the full dataset before splitting leaks test statistics, the classic preprocessing leak.

**EXAM TRAP:** Feature selection removes REDUNDANT (correlated duplicates) and IRRELEVANT (no signal) features — improving speed and interpretability and reducing overfitting — but selection must use TRAINING data relationships only, and removing a feature that only LOOKS useless (interacting with another) damages the model; choosing features by test-set performance is the leakage trap.

**EXAM TRAP:** The CURSE OF DIMENSIONALITY: as dimensions grow, data becomes sparse, distances lose meaning, and models overfit — reduction (feature selection or extraction like PCA) counters it — but reduction trades interpretability and may drop weak-yet-useful signals; equating reduction with deletion of data ROWS (it reduces COLUMNS/features) misstates the operation.

**EXAM TRAP:** Modelling a library system means mapping ENTITIES (book, member, loan) and their RELATIONSHIPS before writing code — the model's quality decides the system's; and every relationship has CARDINALITY (one member borrows many books); skipping cardinality, or modelling the loan as an attribute of book rather than a relationship, are the standard design-model errors.

**EXAM TRAP:** Regression SUMMARISES association — the line minimises squared error — but CORRELATION IS NOT CAUSATION: ice-cream sales and drownings rise together via summer, a confounder; and extrapolating the line beyond the observed x-range predicts nonsense; writing causal claims from an R² or extending predictions far outside the data are the two interpretation traps.

**EXAM TRAP:** Bias enters at EVERY stage — data (unrepresentative sampling), labelling (annotator stereotypes), model (proxy variables like postcode encoding caste), deployment (unequal access) — and MITIGATION must match the stage; testing only the final model for fairness misses data-stage bias, which is exactly where the school-survey example shows bias being born.

**EXAM TRAP:** TRANSPARENCY discloses the system's existence and data; EXPLAINABILITY gives REASONS for a specific output (feature importance, local explanations) — transparency without explainability still hides per-decision logic — and in high-stakes uses (loan denial) explainability is a right, not a courtesy; using the two words interchangeably loses the pillar distinction.

**EXAM TRAP:** The pillars form an AUDIT CHAIN — explainability produces the reason, transparency publishes the process, accountability assigns the OWNER — remove any link and liability evaporates ("the algorithm decided" is not a defence); treating them as three synonyms, or as optional add-ons after deployment, inverts the design order the question rewards.

**EXAM TRAP:** Paradigm choice is a TRADE-OFF on data volume, labels, interpretability, and compute — rule-based for tiny data/maximum explainability, classical ML for labelled tabular data, deep learning for huge unstructured data — and MORE data does not rescue a WRONG paradigm; justifying deep learning for a 50-row spreadsheet is the mismatch the question is built to catch.

**EXAM TRAP:** Deep learning STACKS layers so each refines the representation (edges → shapes → objects) — depth buys abstraction but demands DATA, COMPUTE, and non-linear activations (without which layers collapse into one linear map); and more layers are not automatically better — vanishing gradients and overfitting punish blind depth, which is the trade-off the question tests.

**EXAM TRAP:** Computer vision is a PIPELINE: pixels → preprocessing → feature extraction → decision — raw pixels alone carry no meaning, and every stage's assumptions constrain the next; a model trained on studio-lit faces degrades on sunlight (domain shift) — quoting accuracy without stating the deployment conditions misses the pipeline's end-to-end nature.

**EXAM TRAP:** CV tasks differ by OUTPUT GRANULARITY — classification (whole image, one label), detection (boxes + labels), segmentation (label per PIXEL), tracking (labels across frames) — and difficulty rises with granularity; calling detection "pixel-level" (that is segmentation) or segmentation "box-level" swaps the two hardest-to-distinguish tasks.

**EXAM TRAP:** A CNN applies small LOCAL filters (kernels) as it slides across the image — WEIGHT SHARING means one kernel detects its pattern ANYWHERE (translation tolerance) — and pooling downsamples for tolerance to small shifts; kernels are LEARNED, not hand-drawn, and stacking conv-pool blocks builds hierarchy; saying kernels are manually designed inverts the learning claim.

**EXAM TRAP:** A perceptron computes weighted sum + BIAS, then an ACTIVATION — without the non-linear activation, stacked layers collapse into one linear function — and the perceptron LEARNS by adjusting weights on error (perceptron rule); single-layer perceptrons cannot solve XOR, which is precisely why multi-layer networks exist — omitting the activation or the XOR limit loses the architecture-logic marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** The ML project lifecycle is a CYCLE — problem framing, data, modelling, evaluation, deployment, MONITORING — and evaluation must use metrics MATCHED to the problem (accuracy fails on imbalanced classes; use precision/recall) — and data drift after deployment silently degrades models; ending the lifecycle at deployment is the incomplete answer the question penalises.

**EXAM TRAP:** Guardrails belong IN the lifecycle, not after it — ethical review at framing, consent and bias checks at data, explainability at modelling, audit trails at deployment, and legal compliance (data-protection law) throughout — retrofitting ethics after deployment is costlier and weaker; naming guardrails without mapping them to lifecycle stages loses the integration mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Classical CV separates WHERE (keypoint detection: corners, SIFT-like features) from WHAT (description/matching of those keypoints) — the pipeline matched keypoints across images for stitching and recognition before deep learning — and keypoints must be REPEATABLE under rotation/scale changes; describing keypoint detection as classification (or skipping the repeatability criterion) misses the split the chapter draws.

**EXAM TRAP:** Commerce removes the BARRIERS between producer and consumer — person (transport), place (warehousing), time (storage), risk (insurance), finance (banking), information (advertising) — and each aid maps to ONE barrier; answering with a list of business activities without the barrier-removal logic misses the framework the definition tests.

**EXAM TRAP:** Sole proprietorship's advantages — full autonomy, direct profit, quick decisions, minimal legal formality — are inseparable from its risks: UNLIMITED liability, limited capital, and the business dying with the owner; listing advantages without the liability caveat (or vice versa) gives a one-sided answer where the question explicitly asks for the trade-off.

**EXAM TRAP:** Partnership solves the sole trader's limits — pooled CAPITAL, shared SKILLS, shared RISK, better decisions — but adds unlimited JOINT AND SEVERAL liability and mutual-agency risk (one partner binds all); writing that partnership eliminates personal risk, or that profits split equally by default even with a deed saying otherwise, misreads both the merit and the default rules.

**EXAM TRAP:** Partner TYPES carry different duties: active (manages, unlimited liability), sleeping/dormant (capital only, no management), nominal (lends name only), partner in profits only (no liability for losses) — and every partner is an AGENT of the firm (mutual agency), so one partner's business act binds all; matching type to conduct in the case is where the marks sit.

**EXAM TRAP:** The partnership DEED is optional but decisive — without it, statutory DEFAULTS apply (equal profit share, no interest on capital/salary, 6% on loans) — and REGISTRATION is also optional, but an unregistered firm cannot SUE third parties to enforce contractual rights; claiming the deed or registration is compulsory by law is the standard legal-status error.

**EXAM TRAP:** The company's seven statutory pillars — separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability, transferable shares, common seal, separate property, and incorporation under the Act — work TOGETHER to mobilise public capital; omitting separate legal entity (the foundation the others rest on) or listing features without their capital-mobilisation logic loses the synthesis mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Incorporation creates a SEPARATE JURIDICAL PERSON — the certificate of incorporation is CONCLUSIVE evidence that all registration requirements are met (even if they were not) — and from that date the company can own property, sue, and be sued in its own name; dating the company's legal birth from business commencement (an older requirement) rather than incorporation is the standard error.

**EXAM TRAP:** Unethical decisions cost more than fines — they destroy TRUST across stakeholders (customers switch, investors exit, employees leave, regulators tighten) and the trust deficit outlasts the incident; writing only the immediate legal penalty misses the ripple logic — the stakeholder map (customer, investor, employee, society) is what the answer must walk.

**EXAM TRAP:** E-business scope covers EVERY electronic interaction — B2B, B2C, C2C, INTRA-B (internal), and G2B — not just "selling online"; and it includes internal processes (HR, procurement) that never face a customer; equating e-business with e-commerce (only buying/selling) narrows the scope and loses the classification marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** Payment mechanisms must deliver AUTHENTICATION, confidentiality, integrity, and NON-REPUDIATION — the click-to-buy becomes a transaction only when all four hold; COD persists because trust gaps remain, and gateways sit between buyer-seller-banks; naming only "UPI/cards" without the security properties each mechanism provides misses the infrastructure framing.

**EXAM TRAP:** E-business security is LAYERED — TECHNICAL (SSL/TLS encryption, firewalls), PROCEDURAL (passwords, OTPs, audits), LEGAL (IT Act provisions) — and a layer only as strong as its weakest member: encryption with shared passwords still leaks; answering with technology alone when the question names three layers loses the procedural and legal marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** Q-commerce's differentiator is the 15-20 MINUTE promise, which demands DARK STORES (micro-warehouses near demand), dense SKU selection of essentials, and hyperlocal routing — it is a LOGISTICS model, not just fast delivery; claiming ordinary e-commerce with faster couriers equals q-commerce misses the dark-store infrastructure that the definition hinges on.
